name: Roman army of the Principate

weightNotes.aggression: Goldsworthy (Roman Army at War) stresses the Roman drive to seek battle and win moral dominance; Agricola marched into Caledonia to force Mons Graupius (AD 83). Not 0.9 because frontier policy after Augustus was often containment.
weightNotes.maneuver: Roman battles were won by sustained, methodical infantry pressure and line relief rather than operational manoeuvre (Sabin 2000, Face of Roman Battle); attrition-leaning.
weightNotes.flanking: Auxiliary cavalry on the wings (Mons Graupius: 3,000 cavalry on the flanks per Tacitus) gave a flanking arm, but the decisive arm was frontal infantry.
weightNotes.siegePreference: Conquest was consolidated by systematic sieges: Jerusalem 70, Masada 73/74 (circumvallation and a ramp of about half a million tons of earth), Dacian fortresses 105/106. Field battle still preferred when the enemy offered it.
weightNotes.reserveUse: Tactically the Romans kept strong reserves (Mons Graupius: legions held in reserve in front of the camp while auxilia fought). Strategically the Principate had almost no central reserve, legions sat on the frontiers; 0.35 splits the two.
weightNotes.scouting: Exploratores and speculatores existed, but Teutoburg (AD 9) shows a column marching into an ambush on false intelligence; middling.
weightNotes.retreatThreshold: Basis: share of starting strength lost (killed, wounded, captured, missing) at the moment of withdrawal or break, never the battle total with pursuit. derived:breakpoint-quartile: modelRules.breakpoint.loserCasualtyShareAtBreak.iron high quartile 0.25. Kept under the evidence rule (QA round 4): drill and the relief of the fighting line by fresh ranks and cohorts let Roman formations sustain long fights under loss without breaking (Sabin, JRS 2000; Goldsworthy), holding behaviour on the battlefield. Fortified camps, cited before, bear on recovery after a withdrawal and are no longer part of the basis. No non-backtest battle gives a share at withdrawal.
weightNotes.combinedArms: Legionary heavy infantry with auxiliary cavalry, archers and slingers, field artillery and engineers in one force (Auxilia article; Roman military engineering); Arrian's order against the Alans (AD 135) mixes all four.
weightNotes.initiative: Centurions and legates had local latitude and provincial governors waged war on their own authority, but battle plans were set by the commander; moderate.
weightNotes.logisticsDiscipline: Roth (Logistics of the Roman Army at War) documents granaries, river and sea supply, and the nightly fortified marching camp (Castra article); Romans rarely outran supply.

summary: A long-service professional army of citizen legions (heavy infantry with pilum and gladius) and non-citizen auxilia (cavalry, archers, light and line infantry). On campaign it built a fortified marching camp every night, moved on a supplied road and river network, and fought set-piece battles with auxilia in front or on the wings and legions as the decisive line or reserve. Wars of conquest ended in methodical siege and engineering: circumvallation, ramps, artillery and rams.
whyItWorked: Training, discipline and standardisation let units relieve each other in line and absorb losses that broke citizen and tribal armies. Engineering and logistics let it keep the field year-round, besiege anything and never be caught unfortified at night. Long service gave a deep bench of experienced centurions.
whereItFailed: On the march through forest against an enemy it did not see: Teutoburg (AD 9), three legions lost to Arminius's ambush. Against mobile horse-archer armies on open ground it could not close: Carrhae (53 BC, late Republic, horse archers resupplied by a 1,000-camel train and feigned retreats drawing off Publius Crassus) set the pattern that recurred on the Parthian frontier. Frontier dispersion meant a disaster could not be quickly replaced.
